nodes.title: Prompt Skill.MD (Built for Reference System)
widgets_values:
==================================================

REFERENCE SYSTEM — CRITICAL

==================================================

Characters can use TWO reference systems.

REFERENCE TAGS ARE WORKFLOW REFERENCE TOKENS.

They are NOT ordinary character names.

During processing, a reference tag may be expanded or replaced with detailed reference information.

For example:

^Jerry Seinfeld^

may be transformed by the workflow into reference text similar to:

Jerry Seinfeld played by Jerry Seinfeld on the TV show Seinfeld

Likewise:

{femesole_rachael}

may be transformed into detailed visual-reference information supplied by the user.

Because of this behavior, reference tags must be used deliberately.

A REFERENCE TAG invokes or reinforces a workflow reference.

A PLAIN NAME merely refers to the already-established character in ordinary text.

==================================================

BUILT-IN CHARACTER

==================================================

Visual reference:

^Character Name^

Voice reference:

Character Name

Dialogue:

[English Character Name]Speech…

Example:

^Angelina Jolie^ (S1) says, [English Angelina Jolie]We need to leave.

==================================================

ATTACHED IMAGE/AUDIO CHARACTER

==================================================

Visual reference:

{Character_Name}

Voice reference:

§Character_Name§

Dialogue:

[English §Character_Name§]Speech…

Example:

{BruckBruck} (S1) says, [English §BruckBruck§]We need to leave.

==================================================

HARD MAPPING RULE

==================================================

^Character^ → Character

{Character} → §Character§

The visual reference and voice reference are DIFFERENT tags and must both be preserved exactly WHEN USED.

BUILT-IN:

^Barney Stinson^

must speak with:

Barney Stinson

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, [English Barney Stinson]This is going to be legendary.

ATTACHED REFERENCE:

{femesole_rachael}

must speak with:

§femesole_rachael§

Example:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, [English §femesole_rachael§]Well, I like it.

NEVER write:

[English Barney Stinson]

[English ^Barney Stinson^]

[English {femesole_rachael}]

[English femesole_rachael]

CORRECT:

[English Barney Stinson]Speech.

[English §femesole_rachael§]Speech.

Never mix these systems.

Whenever a supplied reference tag IS invoked, preserve it EXACTLY.

Never replace, rename, normalize, escape, omit, or alter the contents or symbols of an invoked reference token.

The characters:

< >

^

~

{

}

§

/

are meaningful syntax when used in reference or dialogue tags and MUST survive exactly in the generated output.

==================================================

REFERENCE INVOCATION VS ORDINARY CHARACTER MENTION

==================================================

A reference token INVOKES the corresponding workflow reference.

A plain name merely MENTIONS the character.

These are intentionally different operations.

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ stands beside the apartment door.

This invokes and reinforces Barney Stinson’s built-in visual reference.

After the character has been clearly established, ordinary descriptive prose may use a natural name when additional reference reinforcement is unnecessary.

Example:

Barney turns toward the sofa.

This is allowed.

It refers to the already-established physical character without invoking the reference again.

Likewise:

{femesole_rachael} stands beside the kitchen counter.

Rachael looks toward the doorway.

This is allowed.

The first sentence invokes the supplied character reference.

The second sentence refers to the same established character without invoking the reference again.

Reference tokens should be used enough to establish and reinforce identity, but they DO NOT need to replace every occurrence of a character’s name.

Ordinary names are especially useful:

* in natural descriptive prose
* in dialogue spoken by another character
* when repeated reference expansion would be unnecessary
* when the identity of the character is already unambiguous

Do not confuse an ordinary name mention with a new physical character instance.

==================================================

ABSOLUTE RULE — REFERENCE TAGS INSIDE SPOKEN DIALOGUE

==================================================

VISUAL REFERENCE TAGS MUST NEVER APPEAR IN THE ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS OF ….

This includes:

^Character Name^

{Character_Name}

Visual reference tokens may be expanded by the workflow.

If one is placed inside spoken dialogue, the expanded reference description may become part of what the character attempts to say aloud.

WRONG:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, [English Barney Stinson]^Ted Mosby^ stole my tie.

CORRECT:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, [English Barney Stinson]Ted stole my tie.

WRONG:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, [English §femesole_rachael§]I saw ^Barney Stinson^ downstairs.

CORRECT:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, [English §femesole_rachael§]I saw Barney downstairs.

When a character mentions another character while speaking, use the NORMAL HUMAN-READABLE NAME.

==================================================

VOICE TOKENS INSIDE DIALOGUE

==================================================

The speaker’s VOICE TOKEN is REQUIRED inside the dialogue header.

Built-in:

[English Character Name]

Attached:

[English §Character_Name§]

This is metadata selecting the voice.

It is NOT part of the literal spoken sentence.

Everything after the closing ] and before  is literal speech the character should actually say aloud.

NEVER place visual reference tags inside the literal spoken portion.

==================================================

DIALOGUE TAG PRESERVATION — ABSOLUTE

==================================================

EVERY spoken line MUST be wrapped in literal opening and closing dialogue tags:

<d>
</d>

These tags are REQUIRED OUTPUT SYNTAX.

They are NOT optional formatting.

NEVER strip, escape, convert, summarize, or omit  or .

Every opening  MUST have exactly one matching closing .

Only spoken words and the required language/voice metadata belong inside ….

Actions, expressions, camera directions, descriptions, visual reference invocations, and location references MUST remain outside the dialogue tags.

==================================================

LOCATIONS & OTHER REFERENCES

==================================================

Locations, objects, creatures, vehicles, environments, or other supplied references may also use:

{Reference_Name}

These are ALSO workflow reference tokens.

Determine from context whether a {Reference} represents a character or non-speaking asset.

Only characters receive speaker IDs and voice references.

A non-speaking location or object using {Reference_Name} does NOT receive §Reference_Name§ unless it is explicitly established as a speaking character.

Do not unnecessarily redescribe appearance already supplied by a reference.

REFERENCE TOKENS FOR LOCATIONS, OBJECTS, CREATURES, VEHICLES, OR ENVIRONMENTS MUST NOT APPEAR INSIDE ACTUAL SPOKEN DIALOGUE.

WRONG:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, [English Character_A]Let’s go to {New_Location}.

CORRECT:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, [English Character_A]Let’s go to the hotel.

The following NEW prompt may then invoke:

{New_Location}

==================================================

LOCATION CHANGES — ABSOLUTE HARD RULE

==================================================

A PHYSICAL LOCATION CHANGE MAY ONLY OCCUR AT THE BEGINNING OF A NEW PROMPT.

NEVER change physical locations in the middle of a 15-second prompt.

EVERY prompt takes place in exactly ONE physical location.

A prompt may contain multiple camera angles, shots, character movements, or framing changes, but all shots MUST remain within the same physical location.

If the story requires another location:

1. Finish the current prompt entirely inside the current location.
2. End the current prompt normally.
3. Output the prompt separator:

|

4. Begin the NEXT prompt with the literal control marker:

[new_location]

5. Immediately after [new_location], begin:

subject_definitions:

EXACT STRUCTURE:

|
[new_location]
subject_definitions:

The marker:

[new_location]

MUST be the FIRST line of any prompt whose physical location differs from the preceding prompt.

Nothing may appear before [new_location] within that prompt.

Nothing may appear between [new_location] and:

subject_definitions:

[new_location] is a WORKFLOW CONTROL MARKER.

It is NOT:

* a section
* a location reference
* dialogue
* descriptive prose
* a shot instruction

Do NOT put [new_location] inside:

subject_definitions

summary

retention_analysis

detailed_description

overall_soundscape

non_diegetic_music

Do NOT put [new_location] at the END of the previous prompt.

Do NOT place [new_location] immediately before the shot where the change happens.

The change NEVER happens inside a shot.

The NEW prompt begins already in the new location.

==================================================

WHEN TO USE [new_location]

==================================================

Use [new_location] when the physical location changes between prompts.

Example:

Prompt N:

{Apartment}

Prompt N+1:

{Restaurant}

Prompt N+1 MUST begin:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

Use [new_location] even if the same characters appear in both locations.

Use [new_location] even if very little story time has passed.

Use [new_location] whenever the physical environment changes to a genuinely different location.

The FIRST prompt SHOULD normally begin with:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

because it establishes the sequence’s initial physical location.

==================================================

WHEN NOT TO USE [new_location]

==================================================

Do NOT use [new_location] when the next prompt remains in the same physical location.

Do NOT use it merely because:

* the camera angle changes
* the camera moves
* framing changes
* a character crosses the room
* a character enters
* a character exits
* the camera moves from a wide shot to a close-up
* characters move to another part of the same room
* the action continues from another side of the same environment

If Prompt N and Prompt N+1 both occur in {Apartment}, Prompt N+1 begins directly:

subject_definitions:

NOT:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

==================================================

NO MID-PROMPT LOCATION CHANGES

==================================================

A location change MUST NEVER occur in:

[Shot 2]

[Shot 3]

[Shot 4]

or any later shot.

WRONG:

[Shot 1] Inside {Apartment}, Character A talks to Character B.

[Shot 2] At 00:07.000, hard cut to {Restaurant}.

WRONG:

[Shot 1] Character A leaves {Apartment}.

[Shot 2] At 00:08.000, Character A is suddenly inside {Restaurant}.

WRONG:

[Shot 3] Hard scene transition to {New_Location}.

CORRECT:

Finish the entire prompt inside {Apartment}.

Then:

|
[new_location]
subject_definitions:

<Subject 1> is ^Character_A^.

<Subject 2> is {Restaurant}.

…

detailed_description:

[Shot 1] Inside {Restaurant}, ^Character_A^ is already established in the new environment.

If a premise naturally calls for a location change halfway through a planned prompt, SPLIT IT INTO TWO PROMPTS.

Do not compress two locations into one 15-second prompt.

==================================================

REFERENCE REINFORCEMENT

==================================================

Visual reference tokens may be used outside dialogue when useful to reinforce identity.

Useful places include:

* subject_definitions
* summary
* retention_analysis
* initial character establishment
* important shot descriptions
* character re-entry when physically appropriate
* major camera changes
* scenes where identity consistency needs reinforcement

They do NOT need to be inserted into every sentence.

==================================================

CHARACTER CONSISTENCY

==================================================

When clothing is not established by the reference or user, give each character simple scene-appropriate clothing in subject_definitions.

Maintain clothing throughout continuous scenes unless the wardrobe change is visibly performed inside the scene.

Because clips are generated independently, restate important clothing and state information in every prompt.

Clearly establish character geography when relevant:

* LEFT / CENTER / RIGHT
* standing, seated, crouched, etc.
* nearby environmental anchor
* facing direction
* who they look toward
* held objects
* important body/hand positions

Maintain geography between cuts unless movement is explicitly shown.

Ordinary names used after reference establishment always refer to the SAME established physical character unless the scene explicitly introduces another individual.

==================================================

PHYSICAL CHARACTER CONTINUITY — CRITICAL

==================================================

The LAST 22 FRAMES of Prompt N are physically inherited by Prompt N+1 UNLESS Prompt N+1 begins with:

[new_location]

For a SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION, every character visible in those inherited frames already physically exists in the new clip.

They are the SAME physical character instances.

NEVER create, summon, introduce, respawn, duplicate, or re-enter another copy of an inherited character.

If ^Character_A^ is visible at the end of Prompt N, Prompt N+1 MUST treat that visible person as the same ^Character_A^.

If {Character_B} is visible at the end of Prompt N, Prompt N+1 MUST treat that visible person as the same {Character_B}.

An ordinary name referring to that character also represents the SAME physical individual.

For inherited characters, prefer language such as:

^Character_A^ remains standing on the LEFT.

Character A turns toward Character B.

{Character_B} remains seated on the RIGHT.

Character A takes a step forward from their existing position.

ONE CHARACTER REFERENCE = ONE PHYSICAL CHARACTER INSTANCE unless the user explicitly requests duplicates, clones, twins, reflections, screens, photographs, or similar.

==================================================

WARDROBE CHANGES ACROSS CLIPS — CRITICAL

==================================================

A character visible in the inherited LAST 22 FRAMES cannot suddenly have different clothing in a same-location continuation.

If clothing must change, use ONE of these methods:

1. Show the character physically changing clothing.

OR

2. Begin a new prompt with a justified time/state transition.

If that transition ALSO changes physical location, the new prompt MUST begin:

[new_location]

If the wardrobe/time change occurs while remaining in the same location, explicitly establish the time/state jump at the beginning of [Shot 1], but DO NOT use [new_location].

A location change and a time jump may happen together.

In that case:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

…

detailed_description:

[Shot 1] Later that evening inside {New_Location}, the same ^Character_A^ is now wearing a T-shirt.

==================================================

MAXIMUM TWO SPEAKERS — ABSOLUTE HARD RULE

==================================================

ANY NUMBER of characters may appear in a prompt.

A MAXIMUM OF TWO DISTINCT CHARACTERS may produce intelligible speech within one entire 15-second prompt.

THIS LIMIT INCLUDES ALL AUDIBLE SPEECH REGARDLESS OF SOURCE.

This includes:

* on-screen dialogue
* off-screen dialogue
* telephone speech
* television speech
* radio speech
* narration
* whispers
* muttering
* interjections
* shouted words
* intelligible background conversation

Before writing each prompt, silently choose:

S1 = first distinct speaking character

S2 = optional second distinct speaking character

NO THIRD SPEAKER MAY EXIST.

Four or more characters may be present, but only two may speak.

Silent characters may:

* move
* react
* gesture
* eat or drink
* read
* walk
* interact with objects
* perform physical comedy
* interact nonverbally

They MUST NOT produce intelligible speech.

A silent character may become a speaker in a later prompt.

When more than two characters need dialogue, distribute their speaking roles across multiple prompts.

NEVER give a third character even one short spoken line.

NEVER use (S3).

==================================================

SPEAKER IDs

==================================================

Assign speaker IDs by speaking order WITHIN EACH PROMPT.

First distinct speaker:

(S1)

Second distinct speaker:

(S2)

Reuse the IDs throughout that prompt.

NEVER use:

(S3)

(S4)

or any higher speaker ID.

Speaker IDs reset for every new prompt.

Speaker IDs are independent from character reference tags and voice tags.

==================================================

DIALOGUE — CRITICAL

==================================================

EVERY spoken line MUST:

1. Identify the speaking character using the correct visual reference before the dialogue.
2. Include the correct speaker ID.
3. Use “says,”
4. Open with literal .
5. Use the correct language and VOICE reference inside brackets.
6. Include only literal spoken words after the closing ].
7. Close with literal .

BUILT-IN CHARACTER:

^Character Name^ (S1) says, [English Character Name]Speech.

ATTACHED CHARACTER:

{Character_Name} (S1) says, [English §Character_Name§]Speech.

The language may change when explicitly requested.

Otherwise default to:

English

A built-in visual tag ^Character Name^ MUST use the matching Character Name voice tag.

An attached visual tag {Character_Name} MUST use the matching §Character_Name§ voice tag.

NEVER use a visual reference itself as the voice reference.

==================================================

CHARACTER NAMES WITHIN DIALOGUE

==================================================

When the speaker verbally refers to another character, use the character’s NORMAL SPOKEN NAME.

DO NOT use that character’s visual reference token inside the spoken sentence.

CORRECT:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, [English Barney Stinson]Ted, you need to see this.

WRONG:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, [English Barney Stinson]^Ted Mosby^, you need to see this.

The same principle applies to locations, objects, vehicles, creatures, and other workflow references.

Use natural spoken language inside dialogue.

Use workflow reference tokens outside the literal spoken sentence.

==================================================

ACTIONS NEVER GO INSIDE …

==================================================

CORRECT:

^Character Name^ turns toward the door and raises a hand.

^Character Name^ (S1) says, [English Character Name]Wait.

^Character Name^ closes their mouth and looks toward the door.

WRONG:

^Character Name^ (S1) says, [English Character Name]He turns toward the door. Wait.

==================================================

15-SECOND CLIPS

==================================================

Every prompt represents approximately 15 seconds.

EVERY prompt contains exactly ONE physical location.

Prefer 2-5 shots.

[Shot 1] has no timestamp.

Later shots use:

[Shot 2] At 00:05.000, …

Never exceed:

00:15.000

Shot changes may change:

* camera framing
* angle
* composition
* character emphasis
* visible action

Shot changes MUST NOT change physical location.

Keep dialogue concise enough for movement, reactions, pauses, and environmental beats.

Normally finish final dialogue around:

00:11.500-00:13.000

Reserve approximately the final 1-2 seconds for:

* closed mouths
* reactions
* environmental sound
* stable poses
* continuity

==================================================

CROSS-CLIP CONTINUITY — CRITICAL

==================================================

The LAST 22 FRAMES of Prompt N initialize Prompt N+1.

Every “|” is therefore one of THREE boundary types:

A. SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION

B. SAME-LOCATION TIME/STATE TRANSITION

C. NEW-LOCATION TRANSITION

Choose one explicitly during internal planning.

Do NOT treat “|” as merely a text separator.

==================================================

A. SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION

==================================================

Use when location, time, wardrobe, and action continue directly.

DO NOT output:

[new_location]

Prompt N+1 begins directly:

subject_definitions:

Prompt N+1 MUST begin from the exact physical state inherited from Prompt N.

Preserve:

* every visible character
* exact character identity
* number of character instances
* clothing
* LEFT / CENTER / RIGHT geography
* posture
* held objects
* nearby environmental anchors
* general camera relationship

Characters already visible MUST NOT re-enter or be introduced again.

==================================================

SILENT HANDOFF

==================================================

Never end Prompt N with one character actively speaking and immediately begin Prompt N+1 with a different character speaking during a continuation.

Prompt N must end with approximately 1 second where:

* dialogue has finished
* all … dialogue has ended
* mouths are closed
* major gestures settle
* nobody speaks

Prompt N+1 briefly preserves that inherited state before dialogue resumes.

If the next speaker changes, the new speaker performs a visible preparatory action BEFORE speaking.

Useful cues:

* turns
* looks up
* leans forward
* raises a hand
* shifts posture
* takes a step from their existing position
* changes expression

==================================================

B. SAME-LOCATION TIME/STATE TRANSITION

==================================================

Use when the physical location remains the SAME but a meaningful time jump or state change prevents direct visual continuity.

DO NOT use [new_location].

The next prompt still begins:

subject_definitions:

Then establish the time/state transition immediately at the beginning of:

[Shot 1]

Example:

detailed_description:

[Shot 1] Several hours later in the same {Location_Name}, ^Character_A^ now sits alone at the table wearing the changed clothing established in subject_definitions.

Use this only when the location truly remains the same.

==================================================

C. NEW-LOCATION TRANSITION

==================================================

Use whenever the physical location changes.

The previous prompt MUST remain completely inside its original location.

It MUST NOT begin showing the destination.

It MUST NOT transition to the destination in a later shot.

After the previous prompt:

|

The next prompt MUST begin:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

The new prompt’s [Shot 1] begins ALREADY inside the new physical location.

Establish:

* new location
* new composition
* characters present
* character geography
* character orientation
* relevant wardrobe/state
* relevant time jump

DO NOT additionally write:

[Shot 1] Hard scene transition to…

The [new_location] marker already communicates the location boundary.

Instead write the actual new composition directly.

Example:

|
[new_location]
subject_definitions:

<Subject 1> is ^Character_A^, wearing a dark jacket.

<Subject 2> is {New_Location}.

summary:

[reference generation]

…

detailed_description:

[Shot 1] Inside {New_Location}, ^Character_A^ stands on the LEFT near the doorway, facing RIGHT.

This is preferable to:

[Shot 1] Hard scene transition to {New_Location}.

The location transition occurs BEFORE the scene begins, not during Shot 1.

==================================================

STORY STRUCTURE

==================================================

For a typical 4-prompt story:

PROMPT 1 — SETUP

PROMPT 2 — DEVELOPMENT

PROMPT 3 — ESCALATION

PROMPT 4 — PAYOFF

Adjust this structure according to genre and user intent.

For fewer or more prompts, adapt the structure naturally.

If the required story structure needs more location changes than can fit without violating the one-location-per-prompt rule, use additional prompts as necessary.

NEVER combine two locations merely to preserve the requested prompt count.

==================================================

REQUIRED PROMPT FORMAT

==================================================

Every prompt MUST contain these six sections in this exact order:

subject_definitions:

summary:

retention_analysis:

detailed_description:

overall_soundscape:

non_diegetic_music:

[new_location] is a CONTROL MARKER, not a section.

Therefore a new-location prompt has this structure:

[new_location]
subject_definitions:

summary:

retention_analysis:

detailed_description:

overall_soundscape:

non_diegetic_music:

It still contains exactly SIX sections.

A same-location prompt begins directly:

subject_definitions:

==================================================

subject_definitions:

==================================================

Define ONLY references appearing in that prompt.

Example:

<Subject 1> is ^Character_A^, wearing a dark jacket, gray shirt, dark trousers, and black shoes.

<Subject 2> is {Character_B}, maintaining the appearance defined by the supplied reference and wearing a blue jacket.

<Subject 3> is {Location_Name}.

Do NOT substitute the voice reference for the visual reference in subject_definitions.

For a SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION, descriptions must match the inherited character state.

For a NEW-LOCATION TRANSITION, establish the new location and appropriate character state.

==================================================

summary:

==================================================

Begin with:

[reference generation]

Briefly describe the clip using subject labels and visual reference tags when useful for reference reinforcement.

Ordinary character names may also be used when the identity is already unambiguous.

Do not use voice tags in normal summary prose.

Do not place dialogue inside the summary.

Do NOT describe a location change inside summary.

The summary describes ONLY the single location represented by the current prompt.

==================================================

retention_analysis:

==================================================

Include every subject.

For continuous scenes, explicitly preserve the SAME physical character instance inherited from the previous clip.

Ordinary names may refer to these already-established subjects without creating new instances.

For a [new_location] prompt, preserve story-character identity while establishing the character in the newly initialized physical environment.

==================================================

detailed_description:

==================================================

Describe the clip shot-by-shot.

The ENTIRE detailed_description MUST remain in ONE physical location.

Include when relevant:

* camera framing
* location
* character positions
* orientation
* clothing
* movement
* actions
* expressions
* dialogue
* silent reactions
* environmental interaction
* final continuity state

For a continuation, Shot 1 MUST preserve inherited character instances before introducing new movement.

For a [new_location] prompt, Shot 1 immediately establishes the new environment.

NEVER place a location transition in Shot 2 or later.

NEVER write:

[Shot 2] Hard scene transition…

to another location.

If another location is required, finish the prompt and begin another prompt with:

[new_location]

All spoken dialogue MUST use:

…

==================================================

overall_soundscape:

==================================================

Describe appropriate:

* room tone
* environmental ambience
* physical sounds
* object sounds
* footsteps
* audience reactions when appropriate

Do NOT add intelligible background speech unless explicitly requested.

Any intelligible speech still counts toward the ABSOLUTE TWO-SPEAKER MAXIMUM.

==================================================

non_diegetic_music:

==================================================

Describe music when appropriate.

Otherwise:

N/A

==================================================

BOUNDARY PLANNING — CRITICAL

==================================================

Before generating, silently determine for EACH prompt:

LOCATION:

Exactly ONE physical location.

VISIBLE CHARACTERS:

Who physically appears?

PHYSICAL INSTANCES:

Which characters already exist in inherited frames?

REFERENCE INVOCATION:

Which visual references need explicit reinforcement?

VOICE MAPPING:

For every potential speaker, determine their exact visual-to-voice mapping.

S1:

Who is the first speaker?

S2:

Who is the optional second speaker?

SILENT CHARACTERS:

Who remains completely nonverbal?

NEVER assign a third speaker.

DIALOGUE MENTIONS:

Determine whether any speaker verbally mentions:

* another character
* a location
* an object
* a creature
* a vehicle
* another supplied reference

If so, use a NORMAL SPOKEN NAME inside dialogue.

NEVER place that entity’s visual reference token in the actual spoken sentence.

For every “|” determine:

BOUNDARY TYPE:

A. SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION

B. SAME-LOCATION TIME/STATE TRANSITION

C. NEW-LOCATION TRANSITION

END OF PROMPT N:

* location
* time
* visible characters
* exact physical character instances
* clothing
* final speaker
* LEFT / CENTER / RIGHT positions
* posture
* held objects
* mouth states
* final silent buffer

START OF PROMPT N+1:

IF SAME-LOCATION CONTINUATION:

* DO NOT output [new_location]
* preserve physical character instances
* preserve clothing
* preserve geography
* preserve held objects
* begin movement from inherited positions
* never reintroduce an inherited character

IF SAME-LOCATION TIME/STATE TRANSITION:

* DO NOT output [new_location]
* keep the same physical location
* establish the time/state change immediately in Shot 1

IF NEW-LOCATION TRANSITION:

* Prompt N remains entirely in its original location
* Prompt N+1 begins with [new_location]
* [new_location] appears before subject_definitions:
* Shot 1 begins already inside the new location
* establish new geography
* never place the location transition inside a shot

If the location continues AND the first speaker changes:

A SILENT HANDOFF IS MANDATORY.

==================================================

TAG INTEGRITY CHECK — MANDATORY

==================================================

Before returning, inspect EVERY speaking line character-by-character.

For every BUILT-IN speaker, confirm this exact structural pattern:

^Character Name^ (S#) says, [English Character Name]Speech.

For every ATTACHED speaker, confirm this exact structural pattern:

{Character_Name} (S#) says, [English §Character_Name§]Speech.

Then separately inspect the ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS after the closing ].

Confirm that the spoken portion contains NO visual workflow-reference tokens.

Normal human-readable names ARE allowed and expected in spoken dialogue.

Do not allow rendering, formatting, sanitization, markdown conversion, or rewriting to remove required syntax symbols.
